paper_type_evidence.quote: Using the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (VLA) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), we observed 43 sources at 6 and 100 GHz on a timescale of $\sim 1 - 19$ yr post-explosion.
We additionally observed 29 SLSNe with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), seven of which overlap with our VLA sample.

question.value: Search for late-time non-thermal synchrotron radio and millimeter emission from superluminous supernovae (SLSNe) and long gamma-ray bursts (LGRBs) to constrain central engines (magnetar wind nebulae, off-axis relativistic jets), non-relativistic ejecta, fast radio bursts, and obscured star formation in host galaxies.

evidence.quote: We present the largest and deepest late-time radio and millimeter survey to date of superluminous supernovae (SLSNe) and long duration gamma-ray bursts (LGRBs) to search for associated non-thermal synchrotron emission.

Here we present deep late-time radio and mm observations of 43 SLSNe and LGRBs to search for non-thermal synchrotron emission from these sources, which may shed light on their central engines, connection to FRBs, slow ejecta, and host galaxies.

findings_qualitative.value: No late-time radio (6 GHz) or millimeter (100 GHz) emission is detected from the transient positions of 43 SLSNe and LGRBs, aside from the previously reported PTF10hgi and host-galaxy emission from PTF12dam.

evidence.quote: We do not detect radio/mm emission from any of the sources, with the exception of a 6 GHz detection of PTF10hgi (cite: Eftekhari2019), as well as the detection of 6 GHz emission near the location of the SLSN PTF12dam, which we associate with its host galaxy.

findings_qualitative.value: There is no evidence for significant dust-obscured star formation in the majority of SLSN and LGRB host galaxies.

evidence.quote: We find no evidence for significant dust obscuration within the host galaxies.

findings_qualitative.value: Radio and mm upper limits rule out ion-electron magnetar wind nebulae with identical parameters to FRB 121102, but are mostly consistent with scaled-down models tuned to PTF10hgi (with the notable exception of SN2018bsz at 100 GHz).

evidence.quote: Our limits are sufficient to rule out the presence of ion-electron magnetar nebulae with the same parameters invoked for FRB 121102, as they probe luminosities roughly an order of magnitude deeper.

We find that the majority of our limits are consistent with the model light curves invoked for PTF10hgi, although several deep limits at 100 GHz, most notably SN2018bsz with $L_\nu = 7.6\times 10^{26} \rm \ erg \ s^{-1} \ Hz^{-1}$, strongly rule out the presence of such nebulae.

findings_qualitative.value: In electron-positron PWN models, predicted peak radio luminosity is strongly anti-correlated with the magnetar magnetic field B, and the few sources ruled out by current limits are exclusively low-B (B <= 10^14 G) events.

evidence.quote: We find a strong anti-correlation between the peak luminosity and magnetic field, i.e., the more luminous events correspond to lower magnetic fields.
Indeed, the five sources with predicted emission at or above the level of our $3\sigma$ limits correspond to exclusively low-$B$ ($B\lesssim 10^{14}$ G) events.

claims.hypothesis: SLSNe harbor nascent ion-electron magnetar wind nebulae with properties identical to the persistent radio source of FRB 121102.
claims.experiment: Compare 6 GHz VLA and 100 GHz ALMA luminosity upper limits of SLSNe at 1-19 yr post-explosion against Models A and B of Margalit & Metzger (2018) for FRB 121102 and scaled models for PTF10hgi.
claims.result: The 6 and 100 GHz upper limits lie roughly an order of magnitude below the FRB 121102 models (~10^29 erg s^-1 Hz^-1), while remaining mostly above the PTF10hgi models except for SN2018bsz (L_nu = 7.6e26 erg s^-1 Hz^-1).
claims.finding: Ion-electron magnetar nebulae with identical parameters to FRB 121102 are ruled out for this SLSN sample, implying physical differences (e.g., magnetic field strength) between SLSN engines and FRB 121102.

evidence.quote: We find that our limits at both 6 and 100 GHz are sufficient to rule out these models, *with the same parameters as for FRB 121102*.

Finally, the fact that the SLSNe radio limits preclude FRB 121102 models suggests that there may be physical differences (e.g., magnetic field strength) between the magnetar engines responsible for powering SLSNe and that inferred for FRB 121102.

claims.hypothesis: SLSNe produce off-axis relativistic jets that decelerate and become visible at late times in radio and millimeter bands.
claims.experiment: Compare 6 and 100 GHz flux density limits against a grid of Boxfit v2 afterglow light curves (theta_j = 10 deg, theta_obs = 30, 60, 90 deg) and compare minimum jet breakout energies E_min,iso against the observational limits.
claims.result: Limits rule out jets with E_iso >= 10^54 erg for theta_obs <= 60 deg across n ~ 10^-3 - 10^2 cm^-3, and rule out jets above the breakout threshold E_min for 4 VLA sources and 13 ALMA sources (for theta_obs <= 30 deg).
claims.finding: Energetic off-axis jets (E_iso >= 10^54 erg) are largely ruled out, and successful jet breakout is excluded for a subset of SLSNe, while low-energy jets (E_iso <= 10^53 erg) are predicted to fail to break out of the SN ejecta.

evidence.quote: We find that the radio limits largely preclude the presence of jets with $E_{\rm iso}\gtrsim 10^{54}$ erg ($n \sim 10^{-3} - 10^2 \ \rm cm^{-3}$) for $\theta_{\rm obs} = 30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$.
Similarly, among our ALMA sources, we can rule out the presence of off-axis jets at an observer viewing angle $\theta_{\rm obs}\lesssim30^\circ$ for 13 sources

claims.hypothesis: SLSNe are powered by electron-positron pulsar wind nebulae whose radio/mm emission emerges as the ejecta becomes optically thin.
claims.experiment: Compute free-free optical depth with CLOUDY and compare 6 and 100 GHz limits with Boltzmann-equation PWN light curves based on MOSFiT magnetar parameters.
claims.result: Most non-detections are consistent with predicted PWN light curves because they peak at later times (6 GHz) or earlier times (100 GHz) or below sensitivity, but 5 low-B sources (SN2006oz, PTF09cnd, SN2011kf, SN2010gx, SN2007bi) have predicted emission at or above the 3sigma limits.
claims.finding: Standard electron-positron PWN models are consistent with the majority of non-detections, though discrepancies for low-B sources and PTF10hgi's broad SED suggest higher pair multiplicity (gamma_b = 10^4), time-varying ionization, or modified engine parameters.

evidence.quote: For the majority of our sources, we find that the non-detections are consistent with the predicted light curves.
We note that five sources exhibit predicted emission at or above the level of our $3\sigma$ limits at the time of our observations.
A standard electron-positron PWN is unable to explain the observed spectrum for PTF10hgi.

claims.hypothesis: SLSN and LGRB host galaxies harbor substantial dust-obscured star formation.
claims.experiment: Derive obscured SFR upper limits from individual and median-stacked 6 GHz and 100 GHz continuum images and compare them to optically derived SFRs.
claims.result: Only PTF12dam's host is detected (SFR = 6.7 +/- 0.7 M_sun yr^-1, matching optical Halpha SFR = 4.8 +/- 1 M_sun yr^-1), while stacked 3sigma limits give SFR <= 1.7 M_sun yr^-1 (6 GHz SLSNe), <= 27 M_sun yr^-1 (100 GHz SLSNe), and <= 4.2 M_sun yr^-1 (6 GHz LGRBs).
claims.finding: There is no evidence for significant dust obscuration in SLSN and LGRB host galaxies.

evidence.quote: In the case of PTF12dam, our radio detection of the host galaxy corresponds to an SFR of $6.7\pm 0.7 \ \rm M_{\odot} \ yr^{-1}$, comparable to the value inferred from a previous 3 GHz detection ($4.8\pm 0.2 \ \rm M_{\odot} \ yr^{-1}$; (cite: Hatsukade2018)) and an H$\alpha$ measurement, $4.8\pm 1 \ \rm M_{\odot} \ yr^{-1}$ (cite: Perley2016a).
We find no evidence for significant dust obscuration within the host galaxies.

why_this_data.value: Volume-limited VLA sample (z <= 0.35, >= 5 yr post-explosion) and complete accessible ALMA samples (z <= 0.5, >= 3 yr post-explosion in 2017; Decl < 30 deg, z < 0.4 in 2019) to probe late-time synchrotron emission when ejecta become optically thin and off-axis jets decelerate.

evidence.quote: The SLSNe observed with the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (VLA) represent a complete (as of February 2017) volume-limited sample to a distance twice that of FRB 121102 ($z\lesssim 0.35$), and with a timescale of $\gtrsim 5$ years post-explosion, leading to 15 SLSNe.

Events observed during the first campaign (2017.1.00280.S; PI: Berger) constitute all sources accessible to ALMA (as of March 2017) with a timescale of $\gtrsim 3$ years post-explosion and a distance of $z\lesssim 0.5$.

why_this_method.value: Combined 6 GHz and 100 GHz observations probe both GHz-peaking late-time afterglows/nebulae and earlier-peaking millimeter nebulae that experience lower free-free optical depth.

evidence.quote: In each case, the emission is expected to peak in the millimeter on timescales of a few years, and in the GHz regime on timescales of $\gtrsim 10$ yr.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Association of the 3sigma 100 GHz source (55.3 +/- 18.8 uJy) with SN2007bi or its host galaxy was rejected based on astrometric offsets of 1 +/- 0.6 arcsec and 1.5 +/- 0.6 arcsec.

evidence.quote: We find that the millimeter source is offset from the SN position by $1\pm 0.6''$ and is thus unlikely to be related to the SN.
We thus conclude that the weak ALMA detection is unlikely to be related to the SN or the host galaxy.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Association of the 6 GHz emission near PTF12dam with the SN itself was rejected in favor of host galaxy star formation because the radio emission is offset by ~1 arcsec, traces optical host emission, and is resolved out in A-configuration.

evidence.quote: The radio emission is offset from the SN position by $\sim 1$ arcsecond and is instead centered on, and traces, the optical emission from the host galaxy. Thus the emission is most likely related to star formation in the host galaxy

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Marginal 6 GHz detections near SN2009jh (3.6sigma, offset 1.6 arcsec) and GRB 050826 (2.5sigma, offset 1.0 arcsec) were rejected as unlikely to be related to the transients.

evidence.quote: In the case of SN2009jh, the source significance is $3.6\sigma$ ($F_\nu = 23.3\pm 6.4 \ \mu$Jy) but with an offset of $1.6\pm 0.3''$ from the SN position, and we therefore consider it unlikely to be related to the SN.

limitations_admitted.value: Short phased-VLA observation duration (~40 min per source) is prohibitively small for detecting intermittent FRBs.

evidence.quote: Thus, while we are sensitive to the low energy range of FRBs (from FRB 121102), given the intermittent nature of FRB 121102, the short duration of our observations ($\approx 40$ min per source) is prohibitively small.

limitations_admitted.value: ALMA 100 GHz observations are less constraining for obscured star formation rates and late-time off-axis jet afterglows because synchrotron emission peaks at lower (GHz) frequencies on these timescales.

evidence.quote: For the remaining SLSNe in our sample, the radio-inferred SFR limits exceed the optically-inferred rates by factors of $\approx 2-5.2\times 10^3$ (Table [\[tab:master\]](#tab:master)), where the high end is driven primarily by the ALMA 100 GHz observations, which are less constraining in this context.
Because the peak of the afterglow emission is generically at GHz frequencies on such long timescales, our mm limits can accommodate higher jet energies of $E_{\rm iso}\gtrsim 10^{54}$ erg.

limitations_admitted.value: CLOUDY models start at t > 1 yr in the source frame, so 100 GHz free-free transparency timescales shorter than 1 yr (1+z) rely on extrapolations.

evidence.quote: Finally, we report upper limits on $t_{\rm ff, 100GHz}$ for eight sources where $t_{\rm ff, 100GHz} > 1 \rm{yr}$ $(1+z)$, as the `CLOUDY` models start from $t > 1$ yr in the source frame and these results are thus based on extrapolations.

limitations_admitted.value: Seven ALMA-observed SLSNe (LSQ14bdq, SN2015bn, SN2016ard, SN2017jan, SN2018ibb, SN2018hti, SN2018lfe) are expected to still be optically thick to free-free absorption at 100 GHz at the time of observation.

evidence.quote: SN2011kg and LSQ12dlf are expected to be optically thick at the time of our 6 GHz observations, while LSQ14bdq, SN2015bn, SN2016ard, SN2017jan, SN2018ibb, SN2018hti, and SN2018lfe are expected to be optically thick in our 100 GHz observations.

referee_caveats_inferred: The obscured SFR relation used at 100 GHz extrapolates a 1.4 GHz synchrotron power-law (alpha = 0.75) without modeling thermal dust emission, which begins to contribute at 100 GHz.

ALMA beam sizes vary by more than an order of magnitude between the 2017 campaign (~0.25-0.8 arcsec) and the 2019 campaign (~1.5-3.8 arcsec), affecting spatial filtering in host galaxy SFR comparisons and image stacking.

products_in_archive.value: Standard archival ALMA data products were used directly.

evidence.quote: In all cases, we use the ALMA data products, which utilize standard imaging techniques within CASA.

code_released.value: pwkit is publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/pkgw/pwkit).

evidence.quote: Flux densities at the source positions (and image rms values) were extracted using the `imtool` program as part of the `pwkit` package (cite: Williams2017) (Table [\[tab:vla\]](#tab:vla)).

missing_for_reproduction: Exact CLOUDY input scripts and assumed ionizing radiation fraction of magnetar spin-down luminosity
Custom Boltzmann-equation PWN radiative transfer code from Omand et al. (2018) / Murase et al. (2020)
Exact Boxfit v2 configuration files and parameter grid resolution
Exact MOSFiT posterior chains for the newly fitted SLSNe (SN2010kd, SN2016els, SN2017gci, SN2017jan, SN2018hti, SN2018ibb)
reproducibility.estimated_data_volume_inferred: ~5-15 GB for the archival ALMA continuum products and VLA continuum datasets (~50-100 GB if including raw phased-VLA filterbank files).
reproducibility.score_reason: For the ALMA portion, the authors used standard archival pipeline products directly and measured rms/fluxes with a public tool (pwkit/imtool), making the observational measurements trivial to reproduce; however, the downstream theoretical modeling (CLOUDY scripts and custom PWN Boltzmann code) is not fully specified or publicly linked.
reproducibility.rediscovery_reason: Both ALMA project codes (2017.1.00280.S and 2019.1.01663.S) are public in the archive, the authors used the archive pipeline continuum images as-is, and all per-target rms values, 3sigma flux limits, and SFR limits are tabulated in Tables 3 and 4.

methods_papers.why: pwkit package and imtool program used to extract flux densities and image rms values.
Boxfit v2 code used to generate 2D relativistic hydrodynamical off-axis jet afterglow light curves.
MOSFiT code used to fit optical light curves for magnetar and ejecta parameters.
CLOUDY photoionization code used to compute free-free optical depth and transparency timescales.
Radio star formation rate extrapolation formula.

companion_papers.why: Presents the initial 6 GHz detection and 100 GHz upper limit of PTF10hgi obtained as part of this survey.
